extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (PR managers, communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing realistic, measurable public relations objectives (communication, cognitive, attitudinal, behavioral) and for identifying publics via organizational linkages and coorientation. Includes taxonomy of objectives (target, direction, nature) and theoretical criteria (accuracy, understanding, agreement, congruence, hedging/wedging).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congruence
rubrics_metrics.description: Congruence is the extent to which each person thinks the other person’s idea or evaluation is similar to his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs within each party (organization or public) and therefore has less relevance as a communication objective than bilateral measures such as accuracy, understanding, and agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (coorientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy is the extent to which one person’s perception of the other person’s idea or evaluation approximates the other person’s actual idea or evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication between organization and public frequently improves accuracy; example: holding a community meeting can increase an organization's accuracy about public beliefs and evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding (coorientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding represents the extent to which the two ideas are the same (i.e., the extent the organization and public share the same idea about an object).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding may increase when both sides change their ideas after communication (e.g., both come to see the plant will create employment and pollution). Communication increases understanding less often than accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreement represents the extent to which the evaluations (attitudes) are the same between the organization and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement is the most difficult symmetric effect to achieve via communication; research shows communication least often increases agreement compared to accuracy and understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientation model research finding
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication between two parties frequently improves accuracy, less often increases understanding, and least often increases agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because congruency is an intra-person effect, it is less useful as a communication objective. Use coorientation to diagnose which effects (accuracy, understanding, agreement) are realistic objectives for a given situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt coorientation to PR models
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy, understanding, and agreement are important symmetric communication effects that should be major objectives in the two-way symmetric model; other models will have different flows and therefore different likely changes in these effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In two-way asymmetric or one-way models, communication flows primarily from organization to public so only certain effects (primarily public-side changes) will be expected; in two-way symmetric aim for mutual increases in accuracy, understanding, and agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomy of public relations objectives (three dimensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations objectives have three dimensions: Target of the objective; Direction of the effect; Nature of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this taxonomy to choose objectives for a PR program or technique and to evaluate practitioner performance as part of management-by-objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target dimension: External publics and organizational subsystems
rubrics_metrics.description: Targets can be external publics (specific publics generated by a PR problem) or organizational subsystems (e.g., employee publics or subsystems that receive external communication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different objectives may be necessary for each target; publics should be identified specifically (not as a vague 'general public') because publics are defined by a common problem or consequence linking them to the organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction dimension: Asymmetric vs Symmetric effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Asymmetric: the effect is unbalanced and generally the organization attempts to affect publics. Symmetric: the effect is balanced and the relationship between publics and the organization will be affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing direction determines whether objectives aim at changing publics unilaterally (asymmetric) or at mutual change and relationship improvement (symmetric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the effect — Communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The target public or subsystem receives a message (e.g., stories placed in mass media, advertisements, events, brochures, meetings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication as an objective may be sufficient for many PR problems—sometimes a practitioner simply wants to communicate regardless of downstream effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the effect — Retention of Messages (Accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Often called 'accuracy' in the coorientation model: the public or subsystem is exposed to the message and retains it (comprehension), knowing the other's beliefs and evaluations though not necessarily agreeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retention implies recipients remember what was said; it does not imply acceptance or behavioral intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the effect — Acceptance of Cognitions (Understanding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding: the target not only retains the message but accepts it as its beliefs about reality. Targets may hedge or wedge cognitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance is a stronger cognitive objective than mere retention and may be situational—people can hold conflicting beliefs (hedge) or replace one belief with another (wedge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the effect — Formation or Change of an Attitude (Agreement / Behavioral Intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The target should not only believe the message but evaluate its implications favorably and intend to change behavior (attitudinal change / intent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitude change is harder to achieve than cognitive objectives and may be specific to issues (see Fishbein–Ajzen model). It is often appropriate only when necessary for goals such as fundraising, promotion, or lobbying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of the effect — Overt Behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Targets actually change or begin a new or repeated behavior (e.g., write to officials, buy or avoid products, attend events, give money; management may change policy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral objectives are the most difficult to achieve and should be used only when essential; expect relatively low proportions of targets to change behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic expectations about effect magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects become less and less likely as you move from communication to behavior; realistic probabilities guide objective-setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule-of-thumb guidance in the text: expect to communicate with about half of your target group; about half of those communicated with will retain the message; most (70–85%) will have some cognition/attitude; generally no more than ~20% of a target group will engage in any kind of behavior. Use these estimates to set realistic objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for choosing objectives (specificity, situationality, non-connection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Communication effects are specific, situational, and not always connected (i.e., communicating doesn't always leave a message, people may not believe messages or may respond negatively).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talk about the specific problem at hand, be flexible in choosing effects as objectives, and choose different objectives when communicating with different publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hedging and wedging cognitive strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Hedging: people hold two conflicting beliefs about the same issue. Wedging: people hold one belief and reject the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These strategies explain why audiences can hold inconsistent positions across situations; they imply that PR campaigns should not expect to completely replace unfavorable beliefs with favorable ones—more realistically expect hedging (both beliefs held) rather than full replacement. Example: 'Little League Baseball Syndrome' — sponsoring youth activities may create favorable belief but not erase concerns about pollution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define publics by consequences/linkages
rubrics_metrics.description: A public is defined by a common problem or consequence that links an organization and other systems in its environment; publics are specific and can change depending on organizational actions and environmental reactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR managers should determine how organizational consequences 'link' their organization to other systems to identify likely publics and then research those publics to define the exact nature of PR problems and choose realistic objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and matching objectives to publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Be flexible in choosing effects as objectives; different PR problems and different publics call for different effects and strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume one set of objectives fits all publics; choose communication, cognitive, attitudinal, or behavioral objectives depending on the public's activity level, the problem, and the communication model used.
